summary: In this Globes interview during the first week of the October 2023 war in Israel's south, Prof. Leo Leiderman of Bank Hapoalim assesses the likely economic damage and proposes policy responses. He says the war's length and number of fronts will determine the damage, welcomes the Bank of Israel's foreign exchange intervention, and argues a country at war may temporarily raise its deficit and deviate from its inflation target. He urges early, professional, non-politicized planning for post-war rehabilitation and says it is too early to cut interest rates.
one_line: Bank Hapoalim chief economic adviser Leo Leiderman outlines the war's economic risks and proposes a flexible deficit, FX intervention and rehabilitation planning.
key_facts: The Tel Aviv 35 index fell 6.4% over the first week of fighting in the war in Israel's south.
Prof. Leo Leiderman is chief economic adviser at Bank Hapoalim and a professor of economics at Tel Aviv University.
Leiderman has four relatives from Kibbutz Nir Oz who are still missing.
Leiderman says the duration and character of the war will decisively affect the depth of economic damage, and the more fronts, the greater the damage.
He says it is too early to quantify the effect on economic growth in 2024 and 2025, and calls the situation unprecedented compared with the Yom Kippur War, the Lebanon War, two intifadas and Covid.
He expects a substantial decline in private consumption, especially services, and harm to tourism, commerce, transport services, entertainment and restaurants.
Self-employed people and small and medium-size businesses, particularly highly leveraged ones, may be hurt as during the Covid pandemic.
On Monday the Bank of Israel announced a plan to sell $30 billion of its foreign currency reserves to stabilize the shekel, which traded at around NIS 3.96/$.
Leiderman welcomes the decision to extend Amir Yaron's term as Bank of Israel governor at least for the duration of the war, and says the banking system is stable with enough liquidity.
President Biden approved $8 billion in military aid this week, which Leiderman expects will help finance part of the deficit.
Leiderman says there are 'no sacred numbers' for the deficit, whether 3%, 5% or 8% of GDP, but the rise in spending and deficit should be temporary.

He proposes that the Bank of Israel and the Ministry of Finance Budgets Division coordinate post-war rehabilitation planning with research institutes, academics and the private sector, without politicization.
On the next interest rate decision on October 23, Leiderman says it is too early to consider a cut and the current rate is right for the economy.
He says a country at war may temporarily deviate from its inflation target, and that there is currently no surge in inflation expectations.
